thesis.title: Predictivism as a Scope Ambiguity: De Re and De Dicto Confirmation of Searched Hypotheses
thesis.thesis: When a hypothesis H is selected from a large space for its fit to E, E confirms H (de re) exactly as much as it would have if H had been proposed in advance. What E confirms less is the de dicto proposition 'the output of search S is true'. The Bayesian denial of predictivism and the error-statistical affirmation of it are both correct, about different propositions.
thesis.argument_sketch: Distinguish two objects of evaluation: the hypothesis picked out rigidly, and the hypothesis picked out under the description 'whatever S returns on E'. For a coherent agent, P(H|E) is fixed by the prior and likelihood of H and does not depend on how H was found. P(the S-winner is true | E), however, must average over all the hypotheses S could have returned, so it is discounted by the search's reach. I then argue that scientific acceptance, reporting, and policy reliance usually take the de dicto object, because what gets endorsed is the method's verdict. On this reading the physicist's distinction between local and global significance (the look-elsewhere effect) is the same scope distinction. Most canonical predictivist cases have a true de dicto reading and a false de re reading.
thesis.why_new: White (2003), Hitchcock and Sober (2004), and Howson and Urbach each locate the predictive advantage in one place: the predictor's reliability, overfitting, or nowhere. None of them notices that the competing verdicts attach to different propositions. Treating the debate as a scope ambiguity explains why both camps' intuitions are stable, and it gives a principled account of when timing-based judgments are apt.

objection.objection:
The de dicto discount disappears once the agent conditions on her total evidence, so the scope distinction cannot do the reconciling work. After the search has run, the agent knows E and knows that S returned H on E. Given that knowledge, 'the output of S is true' and 'H is true' are equivalent. So P(the S-winner is true | E, S returned H) = P(H | E), and the two objects of evaluation have the same posterior.

The author's discounted quantity comes from 'averaging over all the hypotheses S could have returned.' That average is over counterfactual data and counterfactual outputs. It is a pre-data or unconditional reliability of the procedure, not a credence in a proposition given E. What the thesis calls a scope distinction is really the familiar contrast between a conditional probability and an unconditional error rate. That contrast is the Bayesian/error-statistical dispute itself, restated, not something that dissolves it (Howson and Urbach 2006; Mayo 1996, 2018).

The look-elsewhere effect does not fit the proposed mapping either. In Bayesian analyses of searches such as the Higgs mass scan, the trials factor reappears as prior dilution over the search range, the Occam factor in the Bayes factor. That penalty attaches to the rigidly designated hypothesis 'there is a resonance at m₀,' which is the de re object. So either the search's reach is already in the prior, and the de re posterior is penalized too, contradicting the first half of the thesis. Or the global p-value is a frequentist procedure property that has no de dicto credal counterpart. Either way, local versus global significance is not the de re/de dicto distinction (cf. Gross and Vitells 2010).

Finally, the reconciliation misstates the error statistician's position. Mayo's severity claim is that H itself, de re, has passed a test with low probative capacity. Telling her she is 'correct about a different proposition' assigns her a view she explicitly rejects.
objection.rationale:
The paper's novelty lies entirely in the second half: a de dicto proposition whose confirmation is discounted while de re confirmation is not. The de re half is just standard Bayesian anti-predictivism. If the de dicto posterior collapses into the de re posterior under conditionalization on total evidence, the paper has no distinctive positive claim. The look-elsewhere identification, which is the most interesting application, would also be false as stated.

This is not quite fatal. The author could retreat to the claim that acceptance, reporting, and policy are properly governed by unconditional procedure reliability rather than by posterior credence. That is a substantive normative thesis about which quantity should guide endorsement. But it is a different paper, a defense of a reliabilist or error-statistical norm of acceptance. It would have to argue for that norm against Bayesian decision theory rather than present the dispute as a misunderstanding about scope.

A second escape is to model agents who cannot tractably conditionalize on S's output, making the de dicto quantity a credence for bounded agents. That would need serious development, for example via the old-evidence and logical-omniscience literature (Garber 1983; Hacking 1967). Without one of these moves the central reconciliation fails.

closest_work.work: Maher, P. (1988) 'Prediction, accommodation, and the logic of discovery', PSA 1988 vol. 1; Maher (1990) 'How prediction enhances confirmation', in Dunn & Gupta (eds.), Truth or Consequences
closest_work.relation: The canonical Bayesian predictivism. Successful prediction is evidence that the predictor's *method* is reliable, and only derivatively evidence for the hypothesis. Your de dicto object, 'what S returns is true', is close to Maher's method-reliability proposition. Your de re / de dicto vocabulary relabels his split between the theory and the method that produced it.

closest_work.work: Kahn, J., Landsburg, S. & Stockman, A. (1992) 'On novel confirmation', BJPS 43: 503-516
closest_work.relation: Gives a formal Bayesian model in which novel success raises credence in the scientist or method rather than in the hypothesis as such. Its pattern matches your diagnosis: the hypothesis-level posterior is fixed, and the advantage lives at the level of the generating process.

closest_work.work: White, R. (2003) 'The epistemic advantage of prediction over accommodation', Mind 112: 653-683
closest_work.relation: Locates the predictive advantage in what the prediction reveals about whether the theorist is tracking the truth. White's account is again an advantage attached to the process rather than to the rigidly designated hypothesis. Your thesis needs to say what it adds beyond recasting White's mechanism as a scope distinction.

closest_work.work: Barnes, E. C. (2008) The Paradox of Predictivism, Cambridge UP
closest_work.relation: Distinguishes 'thin' and 'tempered' predictivism and defends the view that prediction confirms via endorsers and their background beliefs. Barnes explicitly frames the debate as a question of which proposition is being confirmed. That framing is the core of your reconciliation.

closest_work.work: Hitchcock, C. & Sober, E. (2004) 'Prediction versus accommodation and the risk of overfitting', BJPS 55: 1-34
closest_work.relation: Recasts predictivism in terms of the estimated predictive accuracy of the *procedure* (Akaike-style) versus support for a fixed hypothesis. This is a direct precedent for the claim that the predictivist and anti-predictivist answer different questions.

closest_work.work: Mayo, D. (1996) Error and the Growth of Experimental Knowledge, chs. 8-9; Mayo (2018) Statistical Inference as Severe Testing, incl. the Higgs/look-elsewhere excursions
closest_work.relation: Mayo argues at length that the likelihood principle makes selection effects ('hunting', 'data-dredging', use-novelty violations) invisible to Bayesian posteriors, while severity, being a property of the testing procedure, registers them. She discusses the LEE explicitly. Her diagnosis of the Bayesian/error-statistical disagreement is essentially yours. She does not concede that both sides are right, but you need to engage her reasons for refusing that concession.

closest_work.work: Staley, K. (1996) 'Novelty, severity, and history in the testing of hypotheses: the case of the top quark', Phil. Sci. 63 (Proc.): S248-S255; Dawid, R. (2017) 'Bayesian perspectives on the discovery of the Higgs particle', Synthese; Cousins, R. (2017) 'The Jeffreys-Lindley paradox and discovery criteria in high energy physics', Synthese
closest_work.relation: These papers already connect tuning, selection, and the look-elsewhere effect in HEP to the prediction/accommodation debate and to Bayesian versus frequentist accounts. Cousins and Dawid show how a Bayesian recovers a trials-factor-like penalty through prior dilution over the search range. That is a *de re* mechanism, and it threatens your identification of the LEE with a scope distinction.

closest_work.work: Scott, J. & Berger, J. (2010) 'Bayes and empirical-Bayes multiplicity adjustment in the variable-selection problem', Annals of Statistics 38: 2587-2619
closest_work.relation: This is the standard statistical treatment of how multiplicity enters a Bayesian analysis: through the prior over the hypothesis space, not through a separate de dicto object. Your account must explain why this is not the right reading of the canonical cases.

novelty.note:
The substance is largely anticipated. The claim that P(H|E) is insensitive to discovery history while prediction confirms something about the method or predictor is the Maher / Kahn-Landsburg-Stockman / White / Barnes line. The claim that error statistics registers selection effects because it evaluates procedures is Mayo's. The reconciliation 'each side is right about a different object' is already explicit in Hitchcock & Sober and implicit in Barnes. What may be new is the de re / de dicto packaging (I know of no paper that uses that apparatus for this purpose, though I cannot rule one out) and the strong claim that scientific acceptance takes the de dicto object.

The argument as sketched has a serious technical gap. For an agent who conditions on E and knows S, the description 'the S-winner on E' picks out H with probability 1. So P(the S-winner is true | E) = P(H | E). The de dicto proposition collapses into the de re one once E is fully conditioned on. Your 'averaging over all the hypotheses S could have returned' is not a posterior on E. It is either (a) a pre-data, unconditional error rate of the procedure, or (b) a posterior on a coarsening of E, such as 'S returned some hypothesis with fit above t'. Your scope distinction is therefore really the old conditional-versus-unconditional divide (cf. Berger & Wolpert, The Likelihood Principle; Kiefer's conditional confidence). That divide is exactly what separates Bayesians from error statisticians. If so, the thesis does not reconcile the two camps. It restates their disagreement as a choice of evaluand, and you must then argue that the coarsened or unconditional object is the right target for acceptance and reporting. Mayo argues for that; Bayesians deny it.

The LEE identification is also contestable. In HEP the trials factor can be reproduced, approximately, by a Bayesian prior spread over the mass range, so no de dicto object is needed. You must show the canonical predictivist cases are not better handled this way.

To claim novelty, you should (1) state precisely which coarsening of E the de dicto posterior conditions on and defend that choice, (2) answer Mayo directly, and (3) show your account classifies some cases differently from Maher, White, and Barnes.

# Two Objects of Evaluation: Selection, Scope, and the Prediction/Accommodation Dispute

## 1. The problem and the proposal

Predictivism is the claim that evidence a hypothesis predicted supports it more than evidence the hypothesis was built or chosen to fit. Bayesians typically deny this (Howson and Urbach 2006). On their view the posterior P(H | e) is fixed by the prior of H and the likelihoods of e under H and its rivals. The history of how H came to be entertained is irrelevant except where it changes those quantities. Error statisticians affirm predictivism, at least for an important class of cases (Mayo 1996, 2018). If a hypothesis is hunted out of a large space because it fits, then the procedure that produced the fit would have produced some fit or other whether or not the output was true. A passing result from such a procedure therefore has little probative force. Particle physicists build the second view into practice. The look-elsewhere effect requires that a bump found by scanning a mass range be assessed by a *global* significance, which is smaller than the *local* significance computed as if the mass had been fixed in advance (Gross and Vitells 2010).

My proposal is that in *selection* cases, where a search S picks a hypothesis from a space Ω because of its fit to data e, there are two objects of evaluation. The first is the selected hypothesis H, picked out rigidly. The second is the proposition that *whatever S returns is true*. The thesis has three parts.

**(T1) De re invariance.** The confirmation e provides for H does not depend on whether H was selected by S or proposed in advance, holding fixed the agent's credences over Ω.

**(T2) De dicto discount.** The confirmation e provides for the proposition that S's output is true is smaller, by a factor I call the *reach* of the search.

**(T3) Allocation.** The Bayesian denial of predictivism is correct about the object in (T1). The error-statistical affirmation, including the physicists' global significance, is correct about the object in (T2). Scientific acceptance, reporting and reliance usually concern the second object.

A referee raised an objection that I take to be the strongest available. Its first part is correct, and I will grant it in full. Once the agent conditions on total evidence, the de re and de dicto propositions have the same posterior. My original formulation put the discount in the posterior of the de dicto proposition, and that was a mistake. The discount lives in *confirmation*, the relation between evidence and the change it makes to a proposition's credibility. Two propositions with the same posterior and different priors are differently confirmed. I will also show that the referee's own recommended move, conditioning on the fact that S returned H, is exactly the operation that produces the de dicto quantity. Section 2 sets up the apparatus and Section 3 states the objection. Sections 4–8 answer its three parts, and Section 9 marks the limits of the view.

## 2. Setup

Let Ω = {H₁, …, Hₙ} be mutually exclusive hypotheses. They need not be exhaustive: there may be a residual possibility H₀, such as "no signal." Let E be the random data, with values e. A search S is a function, known to the agent, from data values to members of Ω. In the actual case the data are e and S(e) = H. Two propositions are relevant.

- **The de re object** is H itself. Its truth at a world does not depend on what data arrive there.
- **The de dicto object** is σ, the proposition that the hypothesis S returns on the data is true. As a set of worlds, σ is the union over i of the propositions [S(E) = Hᵢ ∧ Hᵢ]. At worlds with different data, the truth of σ turns on a different hypothesis. The contrast is the familiar one between "Smith is from Boston" and "the winner of the lottery is from Boston," evaluated when Smith in fact won.

A third proposition does much of the work below:

- **A** = [S(E) = H], the proposition that the search selects H. The actual data entail A.

I measure confirmation by the Bayes factor, the ratio of posterior to prior odds: B(X, e) = O(X | e) / O(X). I write B(X, e | Y) for the same ratio computed relative to background that includes Y. Section 4.3 notes that the direction of every result carries over to the difference and ratio measures (Fitelson 1999).

## 3. The objection

I state the objection at full strength, in three parts.

**(O1) Total evidence.** After the search, the agent knows e and knows that S returned H on e. Given that knowledge, "S's output is true" and "H is true" are equivalent, so P(σ | e) = P(H | e). The discount I attributed to σ came from averaging over the hypotheses S *could* have returned. That average ranges over counterfactual data and counterfactual outputs, so it is a pre-data reliability of the procedure, not a credence given e. What I called a scope distinction is the familiar contrast between a conditional probability and an unconditional error rate. That contrast is the Bayesian/error-statistical dispute itself, restated rather than dissolved.

**(O2) The look-elsewhere effect.** In Bayesian treatments of mass scans, the trials factor reappears as dilution of the prior over the search window, an Occam factor in the Bayes factor. That penalty attaches to "there is a resonance at m₀," which is the rigid, de re hypothesis. This gives a dilemma. Either the reach of the search is already in the de re prior, so the de re posterior is penalized and (T1) is false. Or the global p-value is a frequentist property of the procedure with no credal counterpart. Either way the local/global contrast is not the de re/de dicto contrast.

**(O3) Misattribution.** Mayo's severity claim is that H itself, de re, has passed a test of low probative capacity. Telling her she is right about a different proposition assigns her a view she rejects.

## 4. Posteriors coincide; confirmations do not

### 4.1 The coincidence, granted

**Proposition 1.** P(σ | e) = P(H | e).

*Proof.* The data e entail A. The conjunction of A with σ is equivalent to the conjunction of A with H. Hence σ ∧ e is equivalent to H ∧ e, and the conditional probabilities are equal. ∎

This is (O1)'s first claim. I accept it, and it follows that no coherent agent with the evidence e can have different credences in the two objects. Any version of the thesis that relies on such a difference fails.

### 4.2 Where the discount actually lives

Predictivism, in the Bayesian and error-statistical debates alike, is a claim about *support*: how much e counts in favour of a hypothesis, not how probable the hypothesis ends up. Carnap distinguished confirmation as firmness from confirmation as increase in firmness (Carnap 1962). The prediction/accommodation debate concerns the second. Proposition 1 fixes the posteriors but says nothing about the priors, and the priors of H and σ differ. From Proposition 1 it follows at once that

  B(σ, e) = B(H, e) / ρ, where ρ = O(σ) / O(H).

I call ρ the **reach factor**. In searches over large spaces it is typically much greater than 1. Because the agent did not know where to look, her credence in any particular Hᵢ is spread thin, with O(H) of order 1/n. Her credence that the search's output, whatever it turns out to be, is true equals her expectation of the search's success, which does not shrink like 1/n. A search that scans a thousand cells with reasonable power has a reach factor in the hundreds.

My original sketch said that the de dicto *posterior* is discounted because it averages over what S could have returned. The averaging is real, but it belongs to the de dicto *prior*:

  P(σ) = Σᵢ P(S(E) = Hᵢ ∧ Hᵢ).

Since the posteriors coincide, a larger prior means less confirmation. The corrected thesis holds that e confirms σ less than it confirms H while leaving them equally probable.

### 4.3 Measure-robustness and direction

With the posterior fixed, a proposition with a higher prior is less confirmed on the difference measure, the ratio measure and the likelihood-ratio measure alike. When ρ > 1, (T2) is therefore not an artefact of choosing the Bayes factor. The account also predicts when the asymmetry reverses. If a weak search happens to select a hypothesis that was antecedently more credible than the search's expected success, then ρ < 1, and e confirms the de dicto proposition *more* than the de re one. The predictivist asymmetry is therefore not a law about accommodation as such. It concerns the ratio between the antecedent credibility of a method's output and the antecedent credibility of what the method happened to output. In searches over large, undifferentiated spaces, the cases that motivate predictivism, that ratio is large.

### 4.4 The selection decomposition

(O1) has a second claim: the discounted quantity is a pre-data error rate, not a post-data quantity. To answer it I show that the de dicto confirmation equals a post-data quantity concerning H alone, namely the confirmation e gives H *relative to background that already includes A*.

**Proposition 2.** Suppose two symmetry conditions hold:

- (i) the agent's joint credence over hypotheses and data is invariant under any relabelling of the indices of Ω applied jointly to hypotheses and data, so that she distinguishes candidates only through the data bearing on them;
- (ii) S is equivariant, so that relabelling the data relabels the output.

Then P(A) = 1/n, P(H | A) = P(σ), and P(σ | A) = P(σ). Consequently

  B(H, e) = B(H, A) · B(H, e | A), with B(H, A) = ρ and B(H, e | A) = B(σ, e).

*Proof.* By symmetry each Hᵢ is selected with equal probability, so P(A) = 1/n. Again by symmetry, each term in the sum defining P(σ) is equal, so P(H ∧ A) = P(σ)/n and hence P(H | A) = P(σ). Since σ ∧ A is equivalent to H ∧ A, the same argument gives P(σ | A) = P(σ). The factorization is the chain rule for odds ratios together with the fact that e entails A. Because O(H | A) = O(σ), the second factor equals O(H | e)/O(σ). By Proposition 1 this is O(σ | e)/O(σ) = B(σ, e). ∎

Proposition 2 splits the de re confirmation of H into two factors:

- **(a)** the confirmation H receives from the bare fact that the search selected it;
- **(b)** the confirmation H receives from the rest of the evidence, given that fact.

The de dicto confirmation is exactly (b). The reach factor ρ is exactly (a).

This gives precise content to the old intuition that evidence used to construct a hypothesis cannot also count as independent support for it (Worrall 2014). The use is A, and the independent support is (b). It also shows what each side gets right. The Bayesian is right that (a) is genuine confirmation of H: learning that the maximum excess fell in H's cell is evidence for H. The predictivist is right that (a) is no evidence that *the search got it right*. The search was certain to select something, and under symmetry, the identity of what it selected is irrelevant to whether its selection is correct (P(σ | A) = P(σ)).

Proposition 2 also turns (O1) around. The referee asks us to suppose that the agent knows A. Take that seriously: put A into the background. Relative to that background, e's confirmation of H is B(H, e | A), which is the de dicto value. The posterior is the same whether A is counted as evidence or as background, as it must be. The *support* differs, and the question predictivism asks concerns support. An agent who "already knows that S returned H" and then asks how strongly the data back H is asking for confirmation relative to background including A, and the answer is discounted. The referee's conditioning move does not erase the scope distinction; it produces the de dicto side of it.

Where symmetry fails, the chain rule still holds, and B(H, e | A) = B(σ, e | A), since σ and H are equivalent given A. A may then carry information about σ. For instance, if S lands on a hypothesis the agent already favoured, that bears on whether the search is working. In such cases I take the conditional quantity B(H, e | A) as the general explicans of "support beyond selection." The unconditional B(σ, e) is its special case under symmetry. The symmetric case is the paradigm because uniform priors over a scan window and equivariant algorithms are standard.

### 4.5 Why this is not the dispute restated

The referee's diagnosis is that I have relabelled the contrast between a conditional credence and an unconditional error rate. Three features of the account show otherwise.

First, P(σ) is a *credence*: the agent's prior predictive expectation of the search's success, computed under her own mixture over hypotheses rather than under a fixed null. Bayesians compute such quantities routinely in preposterior analysis and prior predictive checking (Box 1980). Every confirmation measure needs some prior in its denominator; P(σ) is simply the prior of a different proposition.

Second, the discounted quantity B(H, e | A) is a post-data conditional confirmation of H. It mentions no counterfactual outputs except through the probability of A, which is a datum.

Third, the place where the procedure enters is exactly specified, and it does not violate the likelihood principle. Since e entails A,

  B(H, e | A) = LR(e) / LR(A), where LR(A) = P(A | H) / P(A | ¬H).

The total import of e for H is LR(e), which does not depend on the procedure. This is the Bayesian's point, and the account leaves it intact. What the procedure determines is which data values make up A, and therefore how that fixed total divides between "being selected" and "beyond selection." The genuine dispute between the two schools is whether the *total* evidential import of e depends on the procedure. I side with the Bayesian on that. My claim is that the *partition* depends on the procedure, and that the error statistician's verdicts concern the second part of the partition. That is a claim neither school has made, and it is consistent with the likelihood principle.

## 5. A worked case

Consider a scan for a narrow resonance across a mass window divided into n = 1000 resolution cells. The setup is:

- The agent's prior that some resonance lies in the window is 0.5, with location uniform, so P(Hᵢ) = 0.0005 for each "resonance in cell i."
- S returns the cell with the largest local excess.
- Under the agent's prior predictive, if a resonance exists S finds its cell with probability 0.6, so P(σ) = 0.3.
- The prior and the algorithm satisfy the symmetry conditions.
- The data place the largest excess in cell k, large enough that P(H_k | e) = 0.8.

The quantities then come out as follows.

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Prior odds O(H_k) | ≈ 0.0005 |
| Prior odds O(σ) | ≈ 0.43 |
| Reach factor ρ | ≈ 857 |
| Posterior odds O(H_k \| e) = O(σ \| e) | 4 |
| De re Bayes factor B(H_k, e) | ≈ 8000 |
| De dicto Bayes factor B(σ, e) | ≈ 9.3 |
| P(H_k \| A) | 0.3 |

By Proposition 2, learning only that the maximum fell in cell k raises the credence in a resonance there from 1 in 2000 to 3 in 10. Of the total factor of 8000, about 860 is earned by k's being where the search's maximum fell, which was bound to be true of some cell. Only about 9 is support for the proposition that the search found something real.

Now take the counterfactual in (T1). Suppose a theorist with no special information, say one who chose cell k by lottery, had announced k before the data. Her announcement carries no information, so the agent's prior for H_k is still 0.0005, and B(H_k, e) is still 8000. That is (T1).

In this scenario the natural de dicto object is "the theorist's announced cell contains a resonance," and the theorist's procedure does not depend on the data. Across all worlds that proposition is equivalent to H_k, so ρ = 1 and the de dicto confirmation is also 8000. The two scenarios therefore agree de re and disagree de dicto, and the disagreement has a simple source:

- "The bump fell in the theorist's cell" was improbable unless the theorist was right: P(A | σ_T false) ≈ 1/1000, where σ_T is the theorist-indexed proposition.
- "The bump fell in the search's cell" was certain either way.

If we summarize e by the maximal local significance Z, the same structure appears in sampling terms:

- The de re likelihood under falsity, P(Z_k ≥ z | ¬H_k), is approximately the **local** p-value.
- The de dicto likelihood under falsity, P(Z_max ≥ z | ¬σ), is approximately the **global** p-value. It equals it exactly when no resonance exists, and nearly so otherwise.

The slogan "it would have looked this good anyway" is ambiguous in scope. It is false of H_k: had there been no resonance in cell k, cell k would very probably not have shown this excess. It is true of σ: had the search's output been spurious, some cell would very probably still have shown an excess this large.

## 6. The look-elsewhere dilemma answered

**First horn.** (O2) says that if the search's reach is already in the de re prior, the de re posterior is penalized and (T1) is contradicted. The de re *prior* is indeed diluted, in the example to 1 in 2000. But (T1) concerns the Bayes factor, and in any case the dilution is not a penalty *for searching*. It represents the ignorance that made a search necessary. The lottery-theorist scenario has the same dilution, the same Bayes factor and the same posterior. (T1) compares searching with advance proposal *at fixed credences over Ω*, and on that comparison nothing changes.

When advance proposal would have raised the prior, as when a theorist derives the predicted mass from an electroweak fit, the posterior is higher. That difference comes from the theorist's reasons, not from how the data bear on H. It is an evidential difference about H's antecedent credibility, and it falls under the familiar Bayesian treatment of predictivism (Maher 1988; White 2003), which Section 9 sets aside.

**Second horn.** (O2) says that otherwise the global p-value has no credal counterpart. It has one. It is the sampling-theoretic analogue of the denominator of the de dicto likelihood ratio, as Section 5 showed. The Bayesian Occam factor that the referee cites makes the same point from the Bayesian side, once we are careful about *which* hypothesis's Bayes factor carries it. The standard calculation (see Cousins 2017) compares a composite alternative, "there is a resonance somewhere in the window, mass unknown," with background-only. With a uniform mass prior over a window of width Δm and mass resolution δm, this Bayes factor is approximately the maximized likelihood ratio multiplied by an Occam factor of order δm/Δm.

The rigid point hypothesis "there is a resonance at m₀" has, against background-only, a Bayes factor approximately equal to the *local* likelihood ratio, with no Occam factor. For that hypothesis the dilution sits in the prior, not in the Bayes factor. The Occam penalty therefore attaches to the Bayes factor of the *existential* hypothesis, not to that of the rigid one.

The existential hypothesis behaves almost exactly like σ:

- Once the data localize the excess, P(∃ | e) ≈ P(H_k | e) = P(σ | e).
- Antecedently, P(σ) = P(∃) × (the search's power).

So B(∃, e) and B(σ, e) differ only by a factor reflecting the search's power. That factor is of order 1, whereas the factor separating either of them from the rigid Bayes factor is of order n. In the example:

| Hypothesis | Bayes factor |
|---|---|
| Rigid point hypothesis H_k | ≈ 8000 |
| Existential hypothesis ∃ | ≈ 4 |
| De dicto proposition σ | ≈ 9.3 |

The Occam factor separating the rigid from the existential Bayes factor is about 1/2000. The reach factor separating the rigid from the de dicto one is about 1/857. The residual factor of 2.3 is the price of 60% power.

The Bayesian "reappearance of the trials factor" is therefore the de re/de dicto distinction expressed in Bayesian terms. The penalty sits in the Bayes factor of the description-level proposition, which is existential and outcome-indexed, and in the prior of the rigid one. Scott and Berger's (2010) analysis of Bayesian multiplicity adjustment points the same way: multiplicity enters through the prior over which, and how many, effects are real, not through the likelihood of any fixed configuration. (T1) and (T2) are the two sides of that bookkeeping.

I do not claim that the frequentist trials factor and the Bayesian Occam factor are numerically equal. The frequentist factor depends on the significance threshold through the expected number of upcrossings (Gross and Vitells 2010), while the Bayesian one depends on the ratio of resolution to window width. The claim is structural: both discount the same object, the proposition that the search's find is real, and neither discounts the support for the rigid hypothesis.

## 7. Why acceptance, reporting and reliance take the de dicto object

If the posteriors coincide, why does it matter which object is endorsed? It matters because science transmits *support* and not posteriors. An experimental collaboration does not tell readers how probable a resonance is. It reports a strength of evidence, which readers combine with their own priors. The combination is correct only if the reported support and the reader's prior concern the same proposition.

**The double-counting argument.** A typical reader first learns of H through the report. The reader had no credence about cell k as such, and would never have considered it had the search not selected it. The prior the reader brings is a base rate for propositions of the form "the result this kind of analysis turns up is real." That is a prior for σ. By Proposition 2, under symmetry it equals P(H | A): such a reader has in effect already conditioned on A, simply by evaluating the hypothesis that the report presents.

If the analysts report the de re Bayes factor, which includes A's contribution of ρ, the reader counts A twice: once in forming a prior about "the reported finding," and again in the support figure. In the example this would yield posterior odds of 0.43 × 8000 ≈ 3400 instead of 4. The support figure that combines correctly with a σ-prior is B(σ, e). The global significance is its frequentist counterpart. That is why the discount belongs in what gets reported, and it is correct for this reason, not because the local figure misdescribes the bearing of e on H.

The same argument explains when the local figure is the right one to report. A reader who had an independent prior for the specific mass, because a theory predicted it, holds a de re prior and needs the de re support. The major collaborations reported both local and global significances in the 2012 Higgs announcements. On this account, that dual reporting is not an uneasy compromise. It serves readers whose priors attach to different objects.

**Reliance and policy.** Institutional rules have the form "act on outputs of procedure P when statistic T exceeds threshold c." Whether such a rule is a good one depends on how often the outputs it licenses are true, weighted by the stakes. That is a property of σ-type propositions, conditional on the statistic, and it holds whether the rule is assessed by error rates or by Bayesian expected utility. What a policy endorses is the method's verdict, whatever the verdict turns out to be, which is the de dicto object by construction.

**Replication.** The account also explains why fresh data cure selection effects without any change in the support e gave to H. A replication tests the already-identified H on new data e′, with no search over e′. For e′, the selection step plays no role, ρ = 1, and the de re and de dicto confirmations coincide. Once replicated, H detaches from its description. It no longer needs to be evaluated as "the search's output," because there is evidence for it that the search did not use. This is why replication is decisive in practice even though, de re, the original data were already strong support.

Not all acceptance is de dicto. A theorist who takes up H, works out its consequences and assesses its coherence with other physics is evaluating H itself, and the de re support is the right measure of what e contributes to her project. The claim is about the default: in the speech acts and institutional commitments through which findings are transmitted and relied on, the object is the method's verdict.

## 8. The error statistician's own computations

(O3) says that Mayo's severity verdict concerns H itself, so my allocation assigns her a view she rejects. I agree that she would reject the gloss. My claim is that her central counterfactual is true only under the de dicto reading, and that her own requirement in hunting cases is that the de dicto reading be used.

The severity requirement (Mayo and Spanos 2006) says that data x₀ are good evidence for H to the extent that H passes a severe test. That requires two conditions:

- (i) x₀ agrees with H;
- (ii) with very high probability, the test would have produced a result according less well with H than x₀ does, were H false.

In a hunting procedure, "H" inside the counterfactual of (ii) has two readings.

- **Rigid reading.** Were H_k false, would the test very probably have produced a worse fit *to H_k*? In the example, yes. Without a resonance in cell k, cell k would almost never show a 5σ excess. The relevant error probability is the local p-value, and severity is high.
- **Descriptive reading.** Were the hypothesis the procedure outputs false, would the procedure very probably have produced a worse fit *to its output*? No. It would have found some cell with a large excess. The relevant probability is the global one, and severity is low.

Mayo's position on hunting is unambiguous. She holds that the "nominal" error probabilities computed for the selected hypothesis as though it had been fixed in advance are not the "actual" ones, and that selection effects must be included (Mayo 1996, 2018). Her treatment of use-constructed hypotheses (Mayo 1996) holds that hunting matters exactly when it makes it probable that the procedure would output a false hypothesis that passes. Both are descriptive-reading computations. The quantity is the probability that the procedure's output passes while false, which quantifies over what the procedure would have output.

On the rigid reading, her signature claim, that the hunted hypothesis "would have passed even if false," is simply false in cases like the resonance scan. So either the claim has its de dicto content, or it is false. I am not imposing a reading she rejects. I am identifying the reading on which her verdict is true and on which her error probabilities are computed.

What remains disputed is the attribution. Mayo moves from "the test of the procedure's output had low capacity" to "x₀ is poor evidence for H." The Bayesian holds that x₀ gave H a Bayes factor of about 8000. The scope distinction resolves the dispute without declaring either computation wrong:

- x₀ is poor evidence that *the search's verdict* is correct (B(σ, e) ≈ 9).
- x₀ is strong evidence for *H* (B(H, e) ≈ 8000).
- Both parties should give H and σ the same posterior.

The practical recommendations do not conflict, because what an agent should *believe* is fixed by Proposition 1. The disagreement concerns where to locate support, and each side's correct computation supports a claim about a different object.

Mayo's account of harmless use-construction fits this picture. When a procedure is constructed so that its output is rarely false, as with a well-designed estimator, she holds that use-construction does not lower severity. In my terms such a procedure has a high P(σ), so its outputs end up highly credible even though the bare fit gives σ little *additional* support: the fit was guaranteed. Her positive verdicts in these cases also attach to the procedure's reliability, which is a de dicto property. The error-statistical assessment of selected hypotheses is thus uniformly an assessment of the method's output, in both the cases where it penalizes and the cases where it does not.

## 9. Scope and limits

**Selection cases only.** Some canonical predictivist arguments do not concern selection. Maher's (1988) coin-prediction case and White's (2003) analysis of prediction as evidence of reliable theory construction locate the advantage of prediction in the fact that a *successful advance prediction is itself evidence* about the predictor's method, and hence about the theory. In such cases the total evidence differs between the predictor and the accommodator, the de re posteriors genuinely differ, and ordinary Bayesian conditioning accounts for the difference. The scope account neither competes with nor absorbs these cases. My earlier claim that "most canonical predictivist cases" have a true de dicto and a false de re reading should be restricted to cases of selection for fit: data dredging, model search, post hoc subgroup analysis and look-elsewhere scans. Over-fitting arguments (Hitchcock and Sober 2004) occupy a middle position. They concern the predictive accuracy of a *fitted* model, which is a property of the output of a fitting procedure, and so they fit the de dicto template naturally. I do not pursue that here.

**The symmetry conditions.** Proposition 2 requires symmetry in the prior and equivariance in S. Without them, the identity of the selected hypothesis can carry information about the search's success, and B(σ, e) and B(H, e | A) come apart. I have proposed the conditional quantity as the general notion of support beyond selection. Which notion better fits the error statistician's practice in strongly asymmetric searches is a further question. My conjecture is that practice there is unsettled for the same reason the two notions diverge.

**Whether the de dicto object is "really" a proposition.** One may worry that σ, whose content shifts with the data, is a gerrymandered object of credence. It is a perfectly good set of worlds, and agents have attitudes towards such propositions all the time: "whoever wins will be a Bostonian," "whatever the committee decides will be implemented." Its distinctive feature is that the evidence does two jobs: it fixes which hypothesis σ is equivalent to, and it bears on that hypothesis. The de re/de dicto split separates these two jobs. Proposition 2 says that, under symmetry, the first job confirms H without confirming σ.

**Measure sensitivity.** The multiplicative decomposition is specific to odds-based measures. The *ordering*, that σ is less confirmed than H whenever ρ > 1, holds for all standard measures, because the posteriors coincide.

## 10. Conclusion

The referee's objection rests on a correct theorem: conditional on all the evidence, the selected hypothesis and the proposition that the search's output is true are equally probable. My original formulation, which located the discount in the latter's posterior, was wrong. The theorem does not undermine the reconciliation, because the prediction/accommodation dispute concerns support, and equally probable propositions with different priors receive different support.

Under natural symmetry conditions the difference has an exact form. The de re confirmation of the selected hypothesis is the product of two factors:

1. the confirmation it gets merely from having been selected;
2. the confirmation it gets beyond selection.

The de dicto confirmation is the second factor alone. This is what the referee's recommended conditioning on "S returned H" yields when one asks about support rather than credence. The physicists' global significance, and the Bayesian Occam factor that the referee rightly invokes, attach to this de dicto, existential object and leave the rigid hypothesis's Bayes factor untouched. Mayo's actual-versus-nominal error probabilities are de dicto computations, and her counterfactual "it would have passed even if false" is true only under the de dicto reading.

The Bayesian is therefore right that how H was found makes no difference to how strongly e supports H. The error statistician is right that it makes a large difference to how strongly e supports the search's verdict, and the latter is the object that scientific reporting and reliance usually put at stake.

# Two Objects of Evaluation: Selection, Scope, and the Prediction/Accommodation Dispute

## 1. The problem and the proposal

Predictivism is the claim that evidence a hypothesis predicted supports it more than evidence the hypothesis was built or chosen to fit. Bayesians typically deny this (Howson and Urbach 2006). On their view the posterior P(H | e) is fixed by the prior of H and the likelihoods of e under H and its rivals. The history of how H came to be entertained is irrelevant except where it changes those quantities. Error statisticians affirm predictivism, at least for an important class of cases (Mayo 1996, 2018). If a hypothesis is hunted out of a large space because it fits, then the procedure that produced the fit would have produced some fit or other whether or not the output was true. A passing result from such a procedure therefore has little probative force. Particle physicists build the second view into practice. The look-elsewhere effect requires that a bump found by scanning a mass range be assessed by a *global* significance, which is smaller than the *local* significance computed as if the mass had been fixed in advance (Gross and Vitells 2010).

My proposal is that in *selection* cases, where a search S picks a hypothesis from a space Ω because of its fit to data e, there are two objects of evaluation. The first is the selected hypothesis H, picked out rigidly. The second is the proposition that *whatever S returns is true*. The thesis has three parts.

**(T1) De re invariance.** The confirmation e provides for H does not depend on whether H was selected by S or proposed in advance, holding fixed the agent's credences over Ω.

**(T2) De dicto discount.** The confirmation e provides for the proposition that S's output is true is smaller, by a factor I call the *reach* of the search.

**(T3) Allocation.** The Bayesian denial of predictivism is correct about the object in (T1). The error-statistical affirmation, including the physicists' global significance, is correct about the object in (T2). Scientific acceptance, reporting and reliance usually concern the second object.

A referee raised an objection that I take to be the strongest available. Its first part is correct, and I will grant it in full. Once the agent conditions on total evidence, the de re and de dicto propositions have the same posterior. My original formulation put the discount in the posterior of the de dicto proposition, and that was a mistake. The discount lives in *confirmation*, the relation between evidence and the change it makes to a proposition's credibility. Two propositions with the same posterior and different priors are differently confirmed. I will also show that the referee's own recommended move, conditioning on the fact that S returned H, is exactly the operation that produces the de dicto quantity. Section 2 sets up the apparatus and Section 3 states the objection. Sections 4–8 answer its three parts, and Section 9 marks the limits of the view.

## 2. Setup

Let Ω = {H₁, …, Hₙ} be mutually exclusive hypotheses. They need not be exhaustive: there may be a residual possibility H₀, such as "no signal." Let E be the random data, with values e. A search S is a function, known to the agent, from data values to members of Ω. In the actual case the data are e and S(e) = H. Two propositions are relevant.

- **The de re object** is H itself. Its truth at a world does not depend on what data arrive there.
- **The de dicto object** is σ, the proposition that the hypothesis S returns on the data is true. As a set of worlds, σ is the union over i of the propositions [S(E) = Hᵢ ∧ Hᵢ]. At worlds with different data, the truth of σ turns on a different hypothesis. The contrast is the familiar one between "Smith is from Boston" and "the winner of the lottery is from Boston," evaluated when Smith in fact won.

A third proposition does much of the work below:

- **A** = [S(E) = H], the proposition that the search selects H. The actual data entail A.

I measure confirmation by the Bayes factor, the ratio of posterior to prior odds: B(X, e) = O(X | e) / O(X). I write B(X, e | Y) for the same ratio computed relative to background that includes Y. Section 4.3 notes that the direction of every result carries over to the difference and ratio measures (Fitelson 1999).

## 3. The objection

I state the objection at full strength, in three parts.

**(O1) Total evidence.** After the search, the agent knows e and knows that S returned H on e. Given that knowledge, "S's output is true" and "H is true" are equivalent, so P(σ | e) = P(H | e). The discount I attributed to σ came from averaging over the hypotheses S *could* have returned. That average ranges over counterfactual data and counterfactual outputs, so it is a pre-data reliability of the procedure, not a credence given e. What I called a scope distinction is the familiar contrast between a conditional probability and an unconditional error rate. That contrast is the Bayesian/error-statistical dispute itself, restated rather than dissolved.

**(O2) The look-elsewhere effect.** In Bayesian treatments of mass scans, the trials factor reappears as dilution of the prior over the search window, an Occam factor in the Bayes factor. That penalty attaches to "there is a resonance at m₀," which is the rigid, de re hypothesis. This gives a dilemma. Either the reach of the search is already in the de re prior, so the de re posterior is penalized and (T1) is false. Or the global p-value is a frequentist property of the procedure with no credal counterpart. Either way the local/global contrast is not the de re/de dicto contrast.

**(O3) Misattribution.** Mayo's severity claim is that H itself, de re, has passed a test of low probative capacity. Telling her she is right about a different proposition assigns her a view she rejects.

## 4. Posteriors coincide; confirmations do not

### 4.1 The coincidence, granted

**Proposition 1.** P(σ | e) = P(H | e).

*Proof.* The data e entail A. The conjunction of A with σ is equivalent to the conjunction of A with H. Hence σ ∧ e is equivalent to H ∧ e, and the conditional probabilities are equal. ∎

This is (O1)'s first claim. I accept it, and it follows that no coherent agent with the evidence e can have different credences in the two objects. Any version of the thesis that relies on such a difference fails.

### 4.2 Where the discount actually lives

Predictivism, in the Bayesian and error-statistical debates alike, is a claim about *support*: how much e counts in favour of a hypothesis, not how probable the hypothesis ends up. Carnap distinguished confirmation as firmness from confirmation as increase in firmness (Carnap 1962). The prediction/accommodation debate concerns the second. Proposition 1 fixes the posteriors but says nothing about the priors, and the priors of H and σ differ. From Proposition 1 it follows at once that

  B(σ, e) = B(H, e) / ρ, where ρ = O(σ) / O(H).

I call ρ the **reach factor**. In searches over large spaces it is typically much greater than 1. Because the agent did not know where to look, her credence in any particular Hᵢ is spread thin, with O(H) of order 1/n. Her credence that the search's output, whatever it turns out to be, is true equals her expectation of the search's success, which does not shrink like 1/n. A search that scans a thousand cells with reasonable power has a reach factor in the hundreds.

My original sketch said that the de dicto *posterior* is discounted because it averages over what S could have returned. The averaging is real, but it belongs to the de dicto *prior*:

  P(σ) = Σᵢ P(S(E) = Hᵢ ∧ Hᵢ).

Since the posteriors coincide, a larger prior means less confirmation. The corrected thesis holds that e confirms σ less than it confirms H while leaving them equally probable.

### 4.3 Measure-robustness and direction

With the posterior fixed, a proposition with a higher prior is less confirmed on the difference measure, the ratio measure and the likelihood-ratio measure alike. When ρ > 1, (T2) is therefore not an artefact of choosing the Bayes factor. The account also predicts when the asymmetry reverses. If a weak search happens to select a hypothesis that was antecedently more credible than the search's expected success, then ρ < 1, and e confirms the de dicto proposition *more* than the de re one. The predictivist asymmetry is therefore not a law about accommodation as such. It concerns the ratio between the antecedent credibility of a method's output and the antecedent credibility of what the method happened to output. In searches over large, undifferentiated spaces, the cases that motivate predictivism, that ratio is large.

### 4.4 The selection decomposition

(O1) has a second claim: the discounted quantity is a pre-data error rate, not a post-data quantity. To answer it I show that the de dicto confirmation equals a post-data quantity concerning H alone, namely the confirmation e gives H *relative to background that already includes A*.

**Proposition 2.** Suppose two symmetry conditions hold:

- (i) the agent's joint credence over hypotheses and data is invariant under any relabelling of the indices of Ω applied jointly to hypotheses and data, so that she distinguishes candidates only through the data bearing on them;
- (ii) S is equivariant, so that relabelling the data relabels the output.

Then P(A) = 1/n, P(H | A) = P(σ), and P(σ | A) = P(σ). Consequently

  B(H, e) = B(H, A) · B(H, e | A), with B(H, A) = ρ and B(H, e | A) = B(σ, e).

*Proof.* By symmetry each Hᵢ is selected with equal probability, so P(A) = 1/n. Again by symmetry, each term in the sum defining P(σ) is equal, so P(H ∧ A) = P(σ)/n and hence P(H | A) = P(σ). Since σ ∧ A is equivalent to H ∧ A, the same argument gives P(σ | A) = P(σ). The factorization is the chain rule for odds ratios together with the fact that e entails A. Because O(H | A) = O(σ), the second factor equals O(H | e)/O(σ). By Proposition 1 this is O(σ | e)/O(σ) = B(σ, e). ∎

Proposition 2 splits the de re confirmation of H into two factors:

- **(a)** the confirmation H receives from the bare fact that the search selected it;
- **(b)** the confirmation H receives from the rest of the evidence, given that fact.

The de dicto confirmation is exactly (b). The reach factor ρ is exactly (a).

This gives precise content to the old intuition that evidence used to construct a hypothesis cannot also count as independent support for it (Worrall 2014). The use is A, and the independent support is (b). It also shows what each side gets right. The Bayesian is right that (a) is genuine confirmation of H: learning that the maximum excess fell in H's cell is evidence for H. The predictivist is right that (a) is no evidence that *the search got it right*. The search was certain to select something, and under symmetry, the identity of what it selected is irrelevant to whether its selection is correct (P(σ | A) = P(σ)).

Proposition 2 also turns (O1) around. The referee asks us to suppose that the agent knows A. Take that seriously: put A into the background. Relative to that background, e's confirmation of H is B(H, e | A), which is the de dicto value. The posterior is the same whether A is counted as evidence or as background, as it must be. The *support* differs, and the question predictivism asks concerns support. An agent who "already knows that S returned H" and then asks how strongly the data back H is asking for confirmation relative to background including A, and the answer is discounted. The referee's conditioning move does not erase the scope distinction; it produces the de dicto side of it.

Where symmetry fails, the chain rule still holds, and B(H, e | A) = B(σ, e | A), since σ and H are equivalent given A. A may then carry information about σ. For instance, if S lands on a hypothesis the agent already favoured, that bears on whether the search is working. In such cases I take the conditional quantity B(H, e | A) as the general explicans of "support beyond selection." The unconditional B(σ, e) is its special case under symmetry. The symmetric case is the paradigm because uniform priors over a scan window and equivariant algorithms are standard.

### 4.5 Why this is not the dispute restated

The referee's diagnosis is that I have relabelled the contrast between a conditional credence and an unconditional error rate. Three features of the account show otherwise.

First, P(σ) is a *credence*: the agent's prior predictive expectation of the search's success, computed under her own mixture over hypotheses rather than under a fixed null. Bayesians compute such quantities routinely in preposterior analysis and prior predictive checking (Box 1980). Every confirmation measure needs some prior in its denominator; P(σ) is simply the prior of a different proposition.

Second, the discounted quantity B(H, e | A) is a post-data conditional confirmation of H. It mentions no counterfactual outputs except through the probability of A, which is a datum.

Third, the place where the procedure enters is exactly specified, and it does not violate the likelihood principle. Since e entails A,

  B(H, e | A) = LR(e) / LR(A), where LR(A) = P(A | H) / P(A | ¬H).

The total import of e for H is LR(e), which does not depend on the procedure. This is the Bayesian's point, and the account leaves it intact. What the procedure determines is which data values make up A, and therefore how that fixed total divides between "being selected" and "beyond selection." The genuine dispute between the two schools is whether the *total* evidential import of e depends on the procedure. I side with the Bayesian on that. My claim is that the *partition* depends on the procedure, and that the error statistician's verdicts concern the second part of the partition. That is a claim neither school has made, and it is consistent with the likelihood principle.

## 5. A worked case

Consider a scan for a narrow resonance across a mass window divided into n = 1000 resolution cells. The setup is:

- The agent's prior that some resonance lies in the window is 0.5, with location uniform, so P(Hᵢ) = 0.0005 for each "resonance in cell i."
- S returns the cell with the largest local excess.
- Under the agent's prior predictive, if a resonance exists S finds its cell with probability 0.6, so P(σ) = 0.3.
- The prior and the algorithm satisfy the symmetry conditions.
- The data place the largest excess in cell k, large enough that P(H_k | e) = 0.8.

The quantities then come out as follows.

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Prior odds O(H_k) | ≈ 0.0005 |
| Prior odds O(σ) | ≈ 0.43 |
| Reach factor ρ | ≈ 857 |
| Posterior odds O(H_k \| e) = O(σ \| e) | 4 |
| De re Bayes factor B(H_k, e) | ≈ 8000 |
| De dicto Bayes factor B(σ, e) | ≈ 9.3 |
| P(H_k \| A) | 0.3 |

Every figure uses the agent's priors in full. The low base rate of a resonance in any given cell is what makes O(H_k) small, and the posterior of 0.8 is a stipulated outcome of strong data, not an inference that bypasses that base rate.

By Proposition 2, learning only that the maximum fell in cell k raises the credence in a resonance there from 1 in 2000 to 3 in 10. Of the total factor of 8000, about 860 is earned by k's being where the search's maximum fell, which was bound to be true of some cell. Only about 9 is support for the proposition that the search found something real.

Now take the counterfactual in (T1). Suppose a theorist with no special information, say one who chose cell k by lottery, had announced k before the data. Her announcement carries no information, so the agent's prior for H_k is still 0.0005, and B(H_k, e) is still 8000. That is (T1).

In this scenario the natural de dicto object is "the theorist's announced cell contains a resonance," and the theorist's procedure does not depend on the data. Across all worlds that proposition is equivalent to H_k, so ρ = 1 and the de dicto confirmation is also 8000. The two scenarios therefore agree de re and disagree de dicto, and the disagreement has a simple source:

- "The bump fell in the theorist's cell" was improbable unless the theorist was right: P(A | σ_T false) ≈ 1/1000, where σ_T is the theorist-indexed proposition.
- "The bump fell in the search's cell" was certain either way.

If we summarize e by the maximal local significance Z, the same structure appears in sampling terms:

- The de re likelihood under falsity, P(Z_k ≥ z | ¬H_k), is approximately the **local** p-value.
- The de dicto likelihood under falsity, P(Z_max ≥ z | ¬σ), is approximately the **global** p-value. It equals it exactly when no resonance exists, and nearly so otherwise.

The slogan "it would have looked this good anyway" is ambiguous in scope. It is false of H_k: had there been no resonance in cell k, cell k would very probably not have shown this excess. It is true of σ: had the search's output been spurious, some cell would very probably still have shown an excess this large.

## 6. The look-elsewhere dilemma answered

**First horn.** (O2) says that if the search's reach is already in the de re prior, the de re posterior is penalized and (T1) is contradicted. The de re *prior* is indeed diluted, in the example to 1 in 2000. But (T1) concerns the Bayes factor, and in any case the dilution is not a penalty *for searching*. It represents the ignorance that made a search necessary. The lottery-theorist scenario has the same dilution, the same Bayes factor and the same posterior. (T1) compares searching with advance proposal *at fixed credences over Ω*, and on that comparison nothing changes.

When advance proposal would have raised the prior, as when a theorist derives the predicted mass from an electroweak fit, the posterior is higher. That difference comes from the theorist's reasons, not from how the data bear on H. It is an evidential difference about H's antecedent credibility, and it falls under the familiar Bayesian treatment of predictivism (Maher 1988; White 2003), which Section 9 sets aside.

**Second horn.** (O2) says that otherwise the global p-value has no credal counterpart. It has one. It is the sampling-theoretic analogue of the denominator of the de dicto likelihood ratio, as Section 5 showed. The Bayesian Occam factor that the referee cites makes the same point from the Bayesian side, once we are careful about *which* hypothesis's Bayes factor carries it. The standard calculation (see Cousins 2017) compares a composite alternative, "there is a resonance somewhere in the window, mass unknown," with background-only. With a uniform mass prior over a window of width Δm and mass resolution δm, this Bayes factor is approximately the maximized likelihood ratio multiplied by an Occam factor of order δm/Δm.

The rigid point hypothesis "there is a resonance at m₀" has, against background-only, a Bayes factor approximately equal to the *local* likelihood ratio, with no Occam factor. For that hypothesis the dilution sits in the prior, not in the Bayes factor. The Occam penalty therefore attaches to the Bayes factor of the *existential* hypothesis, not to that of the rigid one.

The existential hypothesis behaves almost exactly like σ:

- Once the data localize the excess, P(∃ | e) ≈ P(H_k | e) = P(σ | e).
- Antecedently, P(σ) = P(∃) × (the search's power).

So B(∃, e) and B(σ, e) differ only by a factor reflecting the search's power. That factor is of order 1, whereas the factor separating either of them from the rigid Bayes factor is of order n. In the example:

| Hypothesis | Bayes factor |
|---|---|
| Rigid point hypothesis H_k | ≈ 8000 |
| Existential hypothesis ∃ | ≈ 4 |
| De dicto proposition σ | ≈ 9.3 |

The Occam factor separating the rigid from the existential Bayes factor is about 1/2000. The reach factor separating the rigid from the de dicto one is about 1/857. The residual factor of 2.3 is the price of 60% power.

The Bayesian "reappearance of the trials factor" is therefore the de re/de dicto distinction expressed in Bayesian terms. The penalty sits in the Bayes factor of the description-level proposition, which is existential and outcome-indexed, and in the prior of the rigid one. Scott and Berger's (2010) analysis of Bayesian multiplicity adjustment points the same way: multiplicity enters through the prior over which, and how many, effects are real, not through the likelihood of any fixed configuration. (T1) and (T2) are the two sides of that bookkeeping.

I do not claim that the frequentist trials factor and the Bayesian Occam factor are numerically equal. The frequentist factor depends on the significance threshold through the expected number of upcrossings (Gross and Vitells 2010), while the Bayesian one depends on the ratio of resolution to window width. The claim is structural: both discount the same object, the proposition that the search's find is real, and neither discounts the support for the rigid hypothesis.

## 7. Why acceptance, reporting and reliance take the de dicto object

If the posteriors coincide, why does it matter which object is endorsed? It matters because science transmits *support* and not posteriors. An experimental collaboration does not tell readers how probable a resonance is. It reports a strength of evidence, which readers combine with their own priors. The combination is correct only if the reported support and the reader's prior concern the same proposition.

**The double-counting argument.** A typical reader first learns of H through the report. The reader had no credence about cell k as such, and would never have considered it had the search not selected it. The prior the reader brings is a base rate for propositions of the form "the result this kind of analysis turns up is real." That is a prior for σ. By Proposition 2, under symmetry it equals P(H | A): such a reader has in effect already conditioned on A, simply by evaluating the hypothesis that the report presents.

If the analysts report the de re Bayes factor, which includes A's contribution of ρ, the reader counts A twice: once in forming a prior about "the reported finding," and again in the support figure. In the example this would yield posterior odds of 0.43 × 8000 ≈ 3400 instead of 4. The support figure that combines correctly with a σ-prior is B(σ, e). The global significance is its frequentist counterpart. That is why the discount belongs in what gets reported, and it is correct for this reason, not because the local figure misdescribes the bearing of e on H.

The same argument explains when the local figure is the right one to report. A reader who had an independent prior for the specific mass, because a theory predicted it, holds a de re prior and needs the de re support. The major collaborations reported both local and global significances in the 2012 Higgs announcements. On this account, that dual reporting is not an uneasy compromise. It serves readers whose priors attach to different objects.

**Reliance and policy.** Institutional rules have the form "act on outputs of procedure P when statistic T exceeds threshold c." Whether such a rule is a good one depends on how often the outputs it licenses are true, weighted by the stakes. That is a property of σ-type propositions, conditional on the statistic, and it holds whether the rule is assessed by error rates or by Bayesian expected utility. What a policy endorses is the method's verdict, whatever the verdict turns out to be, which is the de dicto object by construction.

**Replication.** The account also explains why fresh data cure selection effects without any change in the support e gave to H. A replication tests the already-identified H on new data e′, with no search over e′. For e′, the selection step plays no role, ρ = 1, and the de re and de dicto confirmations coincide. Once replicated, H detaches from its description. It no longer needs to be evaluated as "the search's output," because there is evidence for it that the search did not use. This is why replication is decisive in practice even though, de re, the original data were already strong support.

Not all acceptance is de dicto. A theorist who takes up H, works out its consequences and assesses its coherence with other physics is evaluating H itself, and the de re support is the right measure of what e contributes to her project. The claim is about the default: in the speech acts and institutional commitments through which findings are transmitted and relied on, the object is the method's verdict.

## 8. The error statistician's own computations

(O3) says that Mayo's severity verdict concerns H itself, so my allocation assigns her a view she rejects. I agree that she would reject the gloss. My claim is that her central counterfactual is true only under the de dicto reading, and that her own requirement in hunting cases is that the de dicto reading be used.

The severity requirement (Mayo and Spanos 2006) says that data x₀ are good evidence for H to the extent that H passes a severe test. That requires two conditions:

- (i) x₀ agrees with H;
- (ii) with very high probability, the test would have produced a result according less well with H than x₀ does, were H false.

In a hunting procedure, "H" inside the counterfactual of (ii) has two readings.

- **Rigid reading.** Were H_k false, would the test very probably have produced a worse fit *to H_k*? In the example, yes. Without a resonance in cell k, cell k would almost never show a 5σ excess. The relevant error probability is the local p-value, and severity is high.
- **Descriptive reading.** Were the hypothesis the procedure outputs false, would the procedure very probably have produced a worse fit *to its output*? No. It would have found some cell with a large excess. The relevant probability is the global one, and severity is low.

Mayo's position on hunting is unambiguous. She holds that the "nominal" error probabilities computed for the selected hypothesis as though it had been fixed in advance are not the "actual" ones, and that selection effects must be included (Mayo 1996, 2018). Her treatment of use-constructed hypotheses (Mayo 1996) holds that hunting matters exactly when it makes it probable that the procedure would output a false hypothesis that passes. Both are descriptive-reading computations. The quantity is the probability that the procedure's output passes while false, which quantifies over what the procedure would have output.

On the rigid reading, her signature claim, that the hunted hypothesis "would have passed even if false," is simply false in cases like the resonance scan. So either the claim has its de dicto content, or it is false. I am not imposing a reading she rejects. I am identifying the reading on which her verdict is true and on which her error probabilities are computed.

What remains disputed is the attribution. Mayo moves from "the test of the procedure's output had low capacity" to "x₀ is poor evidence for H." The Bayesian holds that x₀ gave H a Bayes factor of about 8000. The scope distinction resolves the dispute without declaring either computation wrong:

- x₀ is poor evidence that *the search's verdict* is correct (B(σ, e) ≈ 9).
- x₀ is strong evidence for *H* (B(H, e) ≈ 8000).
- Both parties should give H and σ the same posterior.

The practical recommendations do not conflict, because what an agent should *believe* is fixed by Proposition 1. The disagreement concerns where to locate support, and each side's correct computation supports a claim about a different object.

Mayo's account of harmless use-construction fits this picture. When a procedure is constructed so that its output is rarely false, as with a well-designed estimator, she holds that use-construction does not lower severity. In my terms such a procedure has a high P(σ), so its outputs end up highly credible even though the bare fit gives σ little *additional* support: the fit was guaranteed. Her positive verdicts in these cases also attach to the procedure's reliability, which is a de dicto property. The error-statistical assessment of selected hypotheses is thus uniformly an assessment of the method's output, in both the cases where it penalizes and the cases where it does not.

## 9. Scope and limits

**Selection cases only.** Some canonical predictivist arguments do not concern selection. Maher's (1988) coin-prediction case and White's (2003) analysis of prediction as evidence of reliable theory construction locate the advantage of prediction in the fact that a *successful advance prediction is itself evidence* about the predictor's method, and hence about the theory. In such cases the total evidence differs between the predictor and the accommodator, the de re posteriors genuinely differ, and ordinary Bayesian conditioning accounts for the difference. The scope account neither competes with nor absorbs these cases. My earlier claim that "most canonical predictivist cases" have a true de dicto and a false de re reading should be restricted to cases of selection for fit: data dredging, model search, post hoc subgroup analysis and look-elsewhere scans. Over-fitting arguments (Hitchcock and Sober 2004) occupy a middle position. They concern the predictive accuracy of a *fitted* model, which is a property of the output of a fitting procedure, and so they fit the de dicto template naturally. I do not pursue that here.

**The symmetry conditions.** Proposition 2 requires symmetry in the prior and equivariance in S. Without them, the identity of the selected hypothesis can carry information about the search's success, and B(σ, e) and B(H, e | A) come apart. I have proposed the conditional quantity as the general notion of support beyond selection. Which notion better fits the error statistician's practice in strongly asymmetric searches is a further question. My conjecture is that practice there is unsettled for the same reason the two notions diverge.

**Whether the de dicto object is "really" a proposition.** One may worry that σ, whose content shifts with the data, is a gerrymandered object of credence. It is a perfectly good set of worlds, and agents have attitudes towards such propositions all the time: "whoever wins will be a Bostonian," "whatever the committee decides will be implemented." Its distinctive feature is that the evidence does two jobs: it fixes which hypothesis σ is equivalent to, and it bears on that hypothesis. The de re/de dicto split separates these two jobs. Proposition 2 says that, under symmetry, the first job confirms H without confirming σ.

**Measure sensitivity.** The multiplicative decomposition is specific to odds-based measures. The *ordering*, that σ is less confirmed than H whenever ρ > 1, holds for all standard measures, because the posteriors coincide.

## 10. Conclusion

The referee's objection rests on a correct theorem: conditional on all the evidence, the selected hypothesis and the proposition that the search's output is true are equally probable. My original formulation, which located the discount in the latter's posterior, was wrong. The theorem does not undermine the reconciliation, because the prediction/accommodation dispute concerns support, and equally probable propositions with different priors receive different support.

Under natural symmetry conditions the difference has an exact form. The de re confirmation of the selected hypothesis is the product of two factors:

1. the confirmation it gets merely from having been selected;
2. the confirmation it gets beyond selection.

The de dicto confirmation is the second factor alone. This is what the referee's recommended conditioning on "S returned H" yields when one asks about support rather than credence. The physicists' global significance, and the Bayesian Occam factor that the referee rightly invokes, attach to this de dicto, existential object and leave the rigid hypothesis's Bayes factor untouched. Mayo's actual-versus-nominal error probabilities are de dicto computations, and her counterfactual "it would have passed even if false" is true only under the de dicto reading.

The Bayesian is therefore right that how H was found makes no difference to how strongly e supports H. The error statistician is right that it makes a large difference to how strongly e supports the search's verdict, and the latter is the object that scientific reporting and reliance usually put at stake.
